## Which papers

The sample is a recency census. For each of the four journals, the most recent online-first articles whose main analysis is statistical on numeric data were taken in order of Crossref online-publication date, cross-checked against OpenAlex. Round one (2026-09-02) took the five most recent per journal, 20 papers. Round two (2026-09-25) took every qualifying article published after each journal's last round-one paper through 2026-09-25: 13 papers (Educational Researcher 5, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis 5, AERA Open 3, American Educational Research Journal 0). One round-two paper (Holtz, AERA Open) has no regression; it is descriptive spatial statistics and is the thinnest quantitative paper in the set. Nothing was excluded after review.

## The two pipelines

Both pipelines use the same six prompts, reproduced below. Each paper receives five sub-reviews, one per dimension, written by separate model sessions that see only the paper and the prompt, followed by a synthesis written by a session that sees the paper, the sub-reviews and the synthesis prompt. The prompts ask for reader-facing guidance about a published paper, not advice to authors.

Claude pipeline. Sub-reviews by Claude Opus (round one) or Claude Opus 5.5 (round two). Synthesis by Claude Fable 5.1. In round two the synthesis session also rendered PDF pages and checked the sub-reviews' specific claims against them, recording each check in a Verification notes section as CONFIRMED, CORRECTED or COULD NOT CHECK. Round-one syntheses were checked against the extracted text only.

Codex pipeline. All sessions run OpenAI GPT-6 (astra) at high reasoning through the Codex CLI (version 0.155.0-alpha.2.6), with the paper's PDF and extracted text and no other information. The Codex reviews were produced after the Claude reviews but with no access to them or to the project's aims. Each Codex synthesis also ends with a Verification notes section.

## Human checks

The site's editor opened the journal pages behind nine of the specific errors the reviews report and confirmed each against the typeset PDF. One of the nine, the Table 2 sums in Ambali et al., was later withdrawn by the mistakes audit: the numbers are as the review describes them, but they do not show an error in the paper. The editor later hand-checked the pages behind the mistakes audit's main findings and the nine example claims on the overreach census page. Nothing else on the site has been human-verified. Two AI readers agreeing is not verification: they read the same extracted text and render the same pages, and can share failure modes.

## Audits after the reviews

Two later audits used the reviews as their starting point. Each has its own page, with its methods, results and quote-free data files.

- [Mistakes audit](mistakes.qmd) (2026-09-26). Every text-versus-exhibit discrepancy the reviews flagged, 141 items, was taken back to the article, the supplements, earlier versions and the authors' data deposits to settle which side is wrong. Seventeen flags were withdrawn. Where the audit showed a statement in a review to be wrong, a dated correction was added to that review and listed on the [Corrections](corrections.qmd) page; where outside evidence changes how a review should be read but no sentence is wrong, a per-paper note was added instead.
- [Overreach census](overreach.qmd) (2026-09-27). Every claim in each paper's title, abstract and closing section was extracted and coded, blind, by two AI coders against a written codebook, to measure how often a paper's headline claims go beyond what its design and evidence support.

## What is not here

The papers themselves are not reproduced; each page links to the article's DOI. Online supplements were not available to either reader except where bound into the PDF, so every claim resting on a supplement is marked as unverifiable in the reviews. The mistakes audit later used the supplements for the 25 papers that have one.
